Usage statistics

mix stats records how Mix is used and reports either dynamic usage or static authorship coverage. Recording is best-effort: a missing, read-only, corrupt, or busy state store never changes program output or exit status.

Collection modes

InvocationModeScript label
interactive REPLinteractivenone
mix file.mixscriptbasename only
mix -c CODEcnone
mix -stdinnone
mix --serve file.mixservebasename only

Calls in functions, callbacks, handlers, source, and include retain the top-level mode and script label. Paths are never stored. Basenames are truncated to 96 Unicode characters; each weekly document keeps at most 128 distinct labels and merges overflow into (other).

The standard prelude and ~/.mixrc load before collection is attached, so bootstrap code does not pollute the invoking program's figures. Remote ssh execution needs no special mode: the far-end process records its normal script, c, or stdin invocation.

Enabled collection is not free. Exact statement/function counts make recursive functions use the canonical evaluator path instead of the native sync-recursion fast path, and tracked calls perform builtin membership lookup. This can be measurable in tight recursive or call-heavy workloads; use MIX_STATS=off when that cost matters.

Disable collection

Set MIX_STATS=off; 0 and false are synonyms, ignoring ASCII case and surrounding whitespace. This is the documented setting for remote and mesh servers:

MIX_STATS=off mix -c 'print("unrecorded")'

The setting is read once per process. When disabled, Mix allocates no collector and opens no state file, database, or lock. Every runtime tracking hook first checks the same cached boolean and returns before borrowing collector state, formatting errors, or scanning builtin names. mix stats, including coverage, prints a disabled message without reading its target.

Storage and concurrency

State lives under $XDG_STATE_HOME/mix, falling back to $HOME/.local/state/mix. One-shot runs accumulate counters in memory and flush once after evaluation, including after exit(code) and ordinary uncaught errors. Long-lived processes retain daily UTC buckets so a run crossing midnight or an ISO-week boundary is split truthfully.

The store is JSONL. A finished run appends one record, its counters by day plus its run record, to runs/YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl, named for the UTC day it was written. That is all a run does with the store: one write(2) on an O_APPEND file, with no lock, no read, no listing and no retry. Each record starts and ends with a newline, so a record a crash or a short write cut short cannot swallow the next one; readers skip blank and unparseable lines, and a complete record that lost only its final newline still counts once. A short or failed write drops that run's counters. Raw files are history: nothing ever rewrites, truncates or deletes them. A file's name says only where a record was written: its buckets and runs carry their own dates, and reports filter by those.

Every record carries a random batch id, and readers keep one copy of each batch per day file (the dedupe does not reach across files). A REPL mix stats pipeline flushes its live counters mid-session and may retry: the retry repeats the same record into the same file. It hands the counters back to the session only when every attempt is known to have written nothing; if an attempt may have landed (an I/O error after the write), they are dropped rather than risk being counted twice. A short write is never retried. A --serve generation retiring at RELOAD is finished, so it is recorded like a run's exit, once.

cache/YYYY-MM-DD.json holds an advisory aggregate per day, with the dates its records touch, written only by mix stats commands, only for days before today, and only when the command gets cache.lock (a busy lock just skips it; runs never touch it). Each entry names the raw file it summarises by device, inode, length, mtime and ctime, all taken from the descriptor that was read, and is fully validated when read. If the raw file no longer matches, because a late run, a clock rolled back or anything else changed it, the entry is ignored and the day is read from the raw file. Deleting cache/ loses nothing.

clear and reset append an operation to ops.jsonl instead of rewriting anything, and apply only to the JSONL store. An operation is anchored to storage positions, not to a clock: it records the length of every raw file when it was issued and applies to exactly the records whose JSON ends within those lengths; anything stored later, in any file, is after it. Operations take ops.lock (runs never do), so two at once take turns, and one refuses if another holds it for two seconds. Repeated operations on the same target (clears of one name, resets of one week) collapse into one when read, which bounds how many a report applies; every report still reads all of ops.jsonl.

Weekly documents from the previous store (current.json, YYYY-WNN.json) are read in place, with that store's own rules, including the fingerprints that stop an interrupted rotation from counting a week twice. They are never moved, rewritten or quarantined, and their writers' lock, stats.lock, is never taken: a binary from before the JSONL store may still be running and writing them, and it drops a write if that lock stays busy. Since it writes only those files while new binaries write only JSONL, the totals add up exactly during a mixed rollout. The documents are read as a validated snapshot: if one changes while it is read (an older binary rotating or rewriting it), the read is repeated, and if it never settles the report says the legacy store was busy. clear and reset refuse, recording nothing, while any of these documents exists: an older binary may still be writing them, so they cannot be cleared exactly. They age out of week windows. The check runs when the operation starts and again once it holds ops.lock; it is a point-in-time check, not proof that no older binary will write one later. mix.db held only what the documents carried and is ignored.

Reports stream: they read each day line by line, use the cache where it still matches (and skip a day whose cached dates miss the window), and keep run records only for reports that list them (sessions, raw, query). Run IDs include 128 bits of random entropy. mix stats commands that get the lock also remove atomic-write temporary files more than an hour old. Details of skipped records are printed only when MIX_DEBUG is set; nothing in collection ever changes a run's output or exit status.

The store is required to be on a responsive local filesystem: appends rely on local O_APPEND semantics (a single write lands whole or is short, never interleaved), and a stalled NFS/FUSE mount can stall a flush.

In script, -c, stdin, and serve modes, SIGINT and SIGTERM take the normal flush path. The interactive REPL stays alive on Ctrl-C and later flushes on EOF, exit, or ordinary shutdown, but an OS SIGTERM uses the terminal process's default termination and may lose its in-memory batch. SIGKILL, a panic, or power loss can also lose the in-memory batch; stats are intentionally best-effort.

If legacy history remains under $MIXOS_SRC/_stats, report commands print a migration or acknowledgement command. History is never moved automatically.

Reports and windows

Every usage report prints its window in the first line. The default window is the current ISO week, and overview and never use the exact same snapshot.

mix stats                 current-week overview
mix stats builtins       current-week builtin calls
mix stats functions      current-week user-function calls
mix stats aliases        current-week alias expansions
mix stats commands       current-week external commands
mix stats keywords       current-week canonical keyword executions
mix stats meta           current-week meta commands
mix stats errors         current-week errors
mix stats sessions       current-week completed runs
mix stats never          current-week builtins and keywords with zero use
mix stats modes          current-week per-mode breakdown
mix stats scripts [N]    top scripts; N defaults to 10 and is bounded to 1–100
mix stats raw            current-week JSON snapshot
mix stats week YYYY-WNN  one ISO week
mix stats since DATE     buckets on or after YYYY-MM-DD
mix stats all            everything recorded
mix stats trend NAME     last 30 recorded days
mix stats query SQL      all-time SQL over an in-memory database

At the interactive REPL, a bare mix stats … line runs in-process and reports this session's live counters. Since 0.61.1 a piped or redirected line (mix stats never | wc -l, mix stats never >> log) runs as a real external pipeline instead — live stats are flushed to disk first, so the child reads current data including this session. Before 0.61.1 the plumbing was silently dropped. See mix man shell-mode § "mix meta-commands under plumbing".

clear NAME removes a name from every counter category of everything stored before it. reset removes the current week's buckets and runs stored before it; older days stay, and a live REPL retains older pending buckets. Both are appended operations, anchored to storage positions and applied at read time; neither rewrites stored data, and runs recorded later keep their counts. Both refuse while the old weekly documents exist (see Storage and concurrency). Week and date arguments must use canonical YYYY-WNN and YYYY-MM-DD forms. query loads everything recorded into an in-memory SQLite database with the tables the old on-disk mix.db had (usage, usage_context, runs, sessions, stats_meta), so existing queries keep working.

The canonical tracked keyword vocabulary is:

if for while loop function return select print eprint parse die
try catch finally export alias break continue send address emit on
source include sh

Structural delimiters such as then, end, done, and each are not usage events.

Static authorship coverage

mix stats coverage DIR

Coverage follows the root path explicitly named by the user, then recursively scans sorted .mix files without following symlinks encountered below that root. It tokenises and parses with Mix's real lexer and parser, then walks the AST. Builtin call sites inside strings, heredocs, or comments cannot be mistaken for code. Nested calls, higher-order builtins, and builtin method syntax are counted. Calls through a function-valued expression are reported as “dynamic calls not classifiable” and are never guessed.

The command reports used and never-authored builtins and canonical keywords. If any selected file is unreadable or fails to lex or parse, diagnostics are printed and the command exits non-zero without emitting a misleading coverage report. Coverage performs no persistence writes.
